changes.why: Brief requires stating the 14-day trial length wherever 'free' appears.

changes.now: Then go and do something better.
changes.why: British English keeps 'go and do' rather than the American 'go do'.
Free trial length must be stated wherever 'free' appears.
"Handled" reads as imported American phrasing in South African English; "sorted" is the everyday local word for something dealt with.
WhatsApp group is the everyday local term for a group chat.
The brief requires stating the 14-day trial length wherever 'free' appears.

flags.text: Check: The CTA says 'Try Kin free' but never states the 14-day trial length as required whenever 'free' appears.
Check: 'chases the refund' and 'finds a time that works for the whole WhatsApp group' imply Kin reads personal messages or accounts, which can invite distrust unless purpose and control are clear.
Check: This is an AI assistant product; the snapshot has no guidance on how such claims are perceived or regulated locally, so the director may want to sanity-check the capability claims.
Check: 'chases the refund' and 'finds a time' imply Kin reads or acts on personal messages/accounts. Data-rights scrutiny is high here unless purpose and control are made clear.
Check: The free trial length is stated but what happens when it ends (auto-renewal, cancellation) isn't, and DMCC rules on this aren't confirmed.
Check: This variant, though matching an approved US version, still needs ARCON Advertising Standards Panel approval before local release.
Check: 'chases the refund' uses a word flagged as regionally ambiguous; confirm it reads naturally rather than oddly literal in Nigerian English.
Check: The copy implies Kin can access personal admin like dentist bookings and group chats; confirm this doesn't read as intrusive data access given fraud sensitivities.
